questions.question: What are Maven's three built-in lifecycles?
questions.title: Maven's Three Lifecycles
questions.direct_answer: Maven has three lifecycles: 'default' (handles project build and deployment), 'clean' (removes build output), and 'site' (generates project documentation).

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Maven's lifecycle model beyond just the default lifecycle
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only knowing the default lifecycle and not knowing 'clean' is a separate lifecycle
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that 'mvn clean package' invokes TWO lifecycles — clean first, then default up to package

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Maven has three built-in lifecycles, each independent from the others. The 'default' lifecycle is the main one — it handles everything from validating the project to deploying the artifact. When developers talk about Maven phases, they almost always mean phases of the default lifecycle. The 'clean' lifecycle has three phases — pre-clean, clean, and post-clean — and its main job is to delete the target/ directory where build outputs live. Running 'mvn clean' removes that directory so you start with a fresh build. The 'site' lifecycle generates project documentation and reports — things like Javadoc, test reports, and code coverage reports in a browsable HTML format. In practice, 'site' is rarely used in modern projects. When you type 'mvn clean package', you're actually invoking two lifecycles in sequence: first the clean lifecycle (removing old build output), then the default lifecycle up through the package phase. This is the most common Maven command pattern because you want to ensure you're building from scratch, not with stale compiled files.

sections.title: Key Points
content: default: compile, test, package, deploy — the main build lifecycle
clean: removes target/ directory — 'mvn clean' ensures a fresh build
site: generates HTML documentation and reports — rarely used in modern CI
'mvn clean package': invokes clean lifecycle first, then default up to package
Lifecycles are independent — running 'package' doesn't trigger 'clean' automatically

sections.hook: Maven doesn't have one lifecycle — it has three. Most developers only know the default one, but knowing all three explains why mvn clean package works the way it does.

beats.label: The three lifecycles:
items: default: the main one — validate, compile, test, package, install, deploy
clean: deletes the target/ directory for a fresh slate (pre-clean, clean, post-clean)
site: generates HTML docs and reports — Javadoc, test results, coverage

beats.content: The three lifecycles are fully independent. Running mvn package does not trigger clean. Running mvn clean does not trigger compile. They're separate execution paths.

non-obvious: when you type mvn clean package, you're invoking two separate lifecycles back-to-back. Maven runs the entire clean lifecycle first, deletes target/, then runs the default lifecycle up through the package phase. That's why it's the standard CI command — always starts from scratch.

sections.cap: Clean, default, site — three independent lifecycles. In daily work you'll use default constantly, clean regularly, and site almost never. But knowing the distinction makes mvn clean package make sense.

questions.question: What are the key phases of Maven's default lifecycle in order?
questions.title: Maven Default Lifecycle Phases
questions.direct_answer: The key phases in order are: validate → compile → test → package → verify → install → deploy — running any phase also runs all preceding phases.

interviewer_intent.testing: Core Maven knowledge — knowing the lifecycle order is essential for understanding Maven commands
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that 'install' puts the artifact in the local ~/.m2 repo, not that it deploys to a server
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the difference between install (local repo) and deploy (remote repo/server) clearly

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The default lifecycle has 23 phases total, but the key ones you need to know are: validate — checks that the project is correct and all necessary information is available. compile — compiles the source code in src/main/java into .class files in target/classes. test — runs the unit tests using a test framework (JUnit, TestNG) via the maven-surefire-plugin. package — takes the compiled code and packages it into a JAR or WAR file in the target/ directory. verify — runs integration tests and checks if the package meets quality criteria. install — copies the JAR or WAR into your local ~/.m2/repository so other projects on your machine can use it as a dependency. deploy — copies the artifact to a remote repository like Nexus or Artifactory for sharing with the team or for production deployment. A critical thing to remember: phases are cumulative. 'mvn install' runs all phases before it — validate, compile, test, package, verify, then install. If your tests fail, the build stops at the 'test' phase and never reaches install.

sections.title: Key Points
content: validate → compile → test → package → verify → install → deploy (key phases in order)
compile: .java → .class files in target/classes
test: runs JUnit tests — if tests fail, build stops here
package: creates JAR or WAR in target/
install: copies artifact to ~/.m2/repository (local cache, not server deployment)
deploy: uploads to remote repository (Nexus/Artifactory) — the 'real' deployment phase

sections.hook: Seven phases. Know them in order and you'll understand exactly what any mvn command does before you run it.

beats.label: Key phases in order:
items: validate: is the project structure correct?
compile: .java files become .class files in target/classes
test: JUnit runs via maven-surefire-plugin; failure stops the build here
package: compile output becomes a JAR or WAR in target/
verify: integration tests and quality checks
install: artifact copied to ~/.m2/repository on your machine
deploy: artifact uploaded to Nexus or Artifactory for the team

beats.content: Phases are cumulative. Running mvn install also runs validate, compile, test, package, and verify first. You never need to chain them manually. If tests fail, the build stops at test and nothing after it runs.

candidates miss: install does NOT deploy the app to a server. It copies the JAR into your local .m2 folder. Deploy is what pushes to Nexus or Artifactory. Neither one runs your application on a server — that's a separate pipeline step.

sections.cap: Memorize the order: validate compile test package verify install deploy. Know that install is for local .m2, deploy is for the shared team repo. Those two trip up a lot of freshers.

questions.question: What are the most commonly used Maven commands and what does each do?
questions.title: Common Maven Commands
questions.direct_answer: 'mvn compile' compiles code, 'mvn test' runs tests, 'mvn package' creates JAR/WAR, 'mvn install' installs to local repo, 'mvn clean' deletes target/, and 'mvn clean package' is the most common full build command.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical hands-on Maven knowledge — these are commands used daily
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that 'mvn package' also compiles and runs tests first — thinking you need three separate commands
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention 'mvn dependency:tree' as a diagnostic command to see all dependencies including transitive ones

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Here are the Maven commands every Java developer uses regularly. 'mvn compile' — compiles your source code, nothing more. Useful for a quick syntax check. 'mvn test' — compiles and runs all unit tests. The build fails if any test fails. 'mvn package' — the full pipeline: compile, test, then package into a JAR or WAR. This is the command you run before deploying. 'mvn install' — same as package but also copies the artifact to your local ~/.m2 cache. Use this when you're building a library that another local Maven project depends on. 'mvn clean' — deletes the target/ directory for a fresh slate. 'mvn clean package' — the workhorse command: clean first (remove old builds), then do the full compile/test/package. Always use clean in CI/CD pipelines. 'mvn clean package -DskipTests' — skip tests for a faster build when you've already verified they pass. 'mvn dependency:tree' — shows the full dependency tree including all transitive dependencies. Invaluable for diagnosing version conflicts. 'mvn spring-boot:run' — runs your Spring Boot application directly from Maven.

sections.title: Key Points
content: 'mvn compile': compile source code only
'mvn test': compile + run unit tests
'mvn package': compile + test + package into JAR/WAR
'mvn install': package + copy to local ~/.m2 repo
'mvn clean package': clean old build + full pipeline — most common CI command
'mvn clean package -DskipTests': skip tests for speed (use sparingly)
'mvn dependency:tree': visualize full dependency tree including transitive deps

sections.hook: A handful of Maven commands will cover 95% of your daily work. Here's the short list every Java developer should know cold.

beats.label: Daily commands:
items: mvn compile — quick syntax check, nothing packaged
mvn test — compiles and runs all unit tests
mvn package — compile + test + produce JAR or WAR
mvn install — package + copy to local ~/.m2 (for local multi-project dev)
mvn clean — delete target/ for a fresh slate
mvn clean package — the CI workhorse: clean then full build
mvn clean package -DskipTests — speed build, skip test execution

beats.label: Diagnostic commands:
items: mvn dependency:tree — full dependency graph including transitive deps
mvn help:effective-pom — see the fully resolved pom Maven actually uses
mvn help:active-profiles — which profiles are on right now

beats.content: candidates miss: mvn package already includes compile and test. You don't need to run them separately. That's the lifecycle model — each phase includes everything before it.

sections.cap: mvn clean package is the command you'll type most in CI. mvn dependency:tree is the one you'll reach for when something breaks. Know both well.

questions.question: How do you skip tests in Maven and when is it appropriate?
questions.title: Skipping Tests in Maven
questions.direct_answer: Use 'mvn package -DskipTests' to skip test execution (but still compile tests), or '-Dmaven.test.skip=true' to skip both compilation and execution — appropriate only in specific scenarios like hotfixes, never as a regular practice.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Maven knowledge plus judgment about when to skip tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Always skipping tests as a habit to make builds faster — this defeats the purpose of testing
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the difference between -DskipTests (compiles tests but doesn't run them) vs -Dmaven.test.skip=true (skips even compilation)

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Maven gives you two ways to skip tests. The first is 'mvn package -DskipTests' — this compiles your test classes but doesn't actually run them. So you catch compilation errors in tests, but you skip the execution time. The second is 'mvn package -Dmaven.test.skip=true' — this skips both compiling and running the tests entirely, which is slightly faster. When is it appropriate to skip tests? Valid scenarios include: you're in a hotfix situation and need to deploy a critical production fix immediately, you know the tests are already passing from a previous build and you just need to repackage, or you're doing a quick local build just to check if your code compiles. However, skipping tests as a regular practice is a bad habit that defeats the purpose of having tests. In CI/CD pipelines, you should almost never skip tests — the pipeline exists specifically to catch regressions before deployment. If your tests are slow, the right solution is to make them faster (use parallel execution, mock external dependencies) rather than skipping them.

sections.title: Key Points
content: '-DskipTests': compiles tests but doesn't run them
'-Dmaven.test.skip=true': skips both compilation and execution of tests
Valid use cases: hotfixes, local quick checks, already-verified builds
Never skip tests in CI/CD pipelines — defeats the purpose of the pipeline
Better solution for slow tests: parallel execution, mocking, or test categorization

sections.hook: Two flags let you skip tests in Maven. They're different in a subtle but important way — and both have a 'use sparingly' asterisk.

beats.content: -DskipTests is the safer option. Your test code still compiles, so you catch compilation errors in tests. It just doesn't execute them. -Dmaven.test.skip=true is slightly faster but skips even compiling tests — so broken test code goes undetected until you re-enable them.
Valid use cases: hotfix deployment where every second counts, quick local repackage when you've just confirmed tests pass, or checking if production code compiles during refactoring.

production trap: skipping tests in CI as a 'speed optimization' is how regression bugs slip to prod. If your tests are slow, fix the speed — parallel execution, better mocking, separating unit from integration tests. Don't skip.

sections.cap: Know both flags. Reach for -DskipTests in valid local dev scenarios. Never make it a CI habit.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'mvn install' and 'mvn deploy'?
questions.title: mvn install vs mvn deploy
questions.direct_answer: 'mvn install' copies the artifact to the local ~/.m2 repository on your machine; 'mvn deploy' uploads it to a shared remote repository (like Nexus or Artifactory) for the whole team or CI/CD system to use.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding that Maven's 'deploy' is not the same as deploying to a server — a very common confusion
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking 'mvn deploy' deploys the application to a production server — it deploys the artifact to a Maven repository
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Clarify that deploying to a server (Kubernetes, EC2, etc.) is done by different tools — Maven deploy is about artifact repositories

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: This is a question where 'deploy' means something different in Maven than it does in general DevOps speak. In Maven's lifecycle, 'install' copies the built artifact (JAR or WAR) into your local Maven repository at ~/.m2/repository. This is useful when you're developing two Maven projects locally and one depends on the other — you 'mvn install' the first project so its artifact is available in your local repo for the second project to pick up as a dependency. 'mvn deploy' takes that artifact and uploads it to a remote Maven repository configured in your pom.xml — typically a company's Nexus or Artifactory server. This makes the artifact available to your entire team, or to CI/CD pipelines that need to resolve it. Note that Maven's 'deploy' has nothing to do with deploying an application to a production server like Kubernetes or AWS. That kind of deployment is handled by separate tools — Maven is just responsible for publishing the artifact to the artifact repository, and then the deployment pipeline picks it up from there.

sections.title: Key Points
content: 'mvn install': artifact → local ~/.m2 repository (your machine only)
'mvn deploy': artifact → remote repository (Nexus/Artifactory — shared with team)
Maven 'deploy' ≠ deploying to a server — it deploys to an artifact/Maven repository
Use install for local multi-module development; use deploy in CI/CD pipelines
Remote repository configured in pom.xml <distributionManagement> section or settings.xml

sections.hook: In Maven, 'deploy' does NOT mean deploying to a server. This trips up freshers constantly. Let's clear it up.

beats.content: Use mvn install when you're developing two Maven projects side-by-side locally. Install project A so project B can pick it up as a dependency from your local .m2 cache. No network needed.
Use mvn deploy in CI/CD. After a successful pipeline run, the artifact gets published to Nexus or Artifactory. Other teams or downstream pipelines can then consume that versioned artifact.

candidates miss: neither install nor deploy runs your application on a server. Deploying to Kubernetes, EC2, or any runtime environment is a completely separate step handled by tools like Helm, ArgoCD, or your CI pipeline.

sections.cap: Install is your local cache. Deploy is the shared team artifact store. Neither one touches a production server.
